Phylogenetic Generalized Linear Mixed Model for Comparative Data

Source: R/pglmm_compare.R
pglmm_compare.Rd

pglmm_compare performs linear regression for Gaussian, binomial and Poisson phylogenetic data, estimating regression coefficients with approximate standard errors. It simultaneously estimates the strength of phylogenetic signal in the residuals and gives an approximate conditional likelihood ratio test for the hypothesis that there is no signal (returned as LRT, see Details). Therefore, when applied without predictor (independent) variables, it gives a test for phylogenetic signal. pglmm_compare is a wrapper for pglmm tailored for comparative data in which each value of the response (dependent) variable corresponds to a single tip on a phylogenetic tree. If there are multiple measures for each species, pglmm will be helpful.

Usage

pglmm_compare(
  formula,
  family = "gaussian",
  data = list(),
  phy,
  REML = TRUE,
  optimizer = NULL,
  add.obs.re = TRUE,
  verbose = FALSE,
  cpp = TRUE,
  bayes = FALSE,
  reltol = 10^-6,
  maxit = 500,
  tol.pql = 10^-6,
  maxit.pql = 200,
  marginal.summ = "mean",
  calc.DIC = TRUE,
  prior = "inla.default",
  prior_alpha = 0.1,
  prior_mu = 1,
  ML.init = FALSE,
  s2.init = 1,
  B.init = NULL,
  calc.WAIC = TRUE,
  bayes_options = NULL,
  posterior.sample = TRUE,
  return.fitted.marginals = TRUE,
  sparse = NULL,
  standardize_cov = TRUE,
  method = c("Laplace", "PQL")
)

# S3 method for class 'pglmm_compare'
predict(object, newdata = NULL, ...)

Arguments

formula

A two-sided linear formula object describing the fixed-effects of the model; for example, Y ~ X. Binomial data can be either presence/absence, or a two-column array of 'successes' and 'failures'. The phylogenetic random term is added automatically; the formula must not have random terms. Offsets (e.g. + offset(log(area))) are supported with method = "Laplace" and bayes = TRUE.

family

Either "gaussian" for a Linear Mixed Model, or "binomial", "poisson", "nbinomial" (negative binomial) or "Gamma" for Generalized Linear Mixed Models. family should be specified as a character string (i.e., quoted). For binomial and Poisson data, we use the canonical logit and log link functions, respectively; negative binomial and Gamma data use the log link (see pglmm()). Binomial data can be either presence/absence, or a two-column array of 'successes' and 'failures'. If bayes = TRUE there are three additional families available: "zeroinflated.binomial", "zeroinflated.poisson" and "zeroinflated.nbinomial", which add a zero inflation parameter; this parameter gives the probability that the response is a zero. The rest of the parameters of the model then reflect the "non-zero" part of the model. Note that "zeroinflated.binomial" only makes sense for success/failure response data.

data

A data frame containing the variables named in formula. It must has the tip labels of the phylogeny as row names; if they are not in the same order, the data frame will be arranged so that row names match the order of tip labels.

phy

A phylogenetic tree as an object of class "phylo".

REML

Whether REML or ML is used for model fitting the random effects. Ignored if bayes = TRUE. For binomial and poisson models with method = "Laplace", REML = TRUE integrates the fixed effects out of the likelihood with the Laplace approximation too (as glmmTMB(REML = TRUE)); use REML = FALSE for maximum likelihood estimates, comparable with lme4::glmer() and glmmTMB().

optimizer

Optimizer to use. Options: "lbfgs" (L-BFGS with analytic gradient; default for Gaussian, also available for binomial/Poisson), "nelder-mead-nlopt" (default for binomial/Poisson), "bobyqa", "Nelder-Mead", or "subplex". "Nelder-Mead" is from the stats package; all others are from the nloptr package. With sparse = TRUE, the default (and "lbfgs") is nlminb() with the analytic gradient of the likelihood (see sparse); "subplex", "nelder-mead-nlopt", "Nelder-Mead" (both the Nelder-Mead algorithm of nloptr) and "bobyqa" are derivative-free, and the optimizer is restarted from its solution until the likelihood does not improve (for gaussian models; for binomial and poisson models, each PQL iteration already starts the optimizer from the previous solution). Ignored if bayes = TRUE or method = "Laplace".

add.obs.re

Whether to add an observation-level random term 1|obs for Poisson data and binomial data with more than one trial (a non-phylogenetic variance, which accounts for overdispersion). The default is TRUE, as in pglmm(): without it, overdispersion is absorbed by the phylogenetic variance, which inflates the phylogenetic signal and its test. It is not used for gaussian data (the residual variance plays this role) or binary data. Earlier versions ignored this argument, so set add.obs.re = FALSE to get their estimates.

verbose

If TRUE, the model deviance and running estimates of s2 and B are plotted each iteration during optimization.

cpp

Whether to use C++ function for optim. Default is TRUE. Only used by the dense code (sparse = FALSE, which is the default only for models that the sparse code does not support, see sparse); ignored if bayes = TRUE, sparse = TRUE or method = "Laplace" (and thus for family = "nbinomial" and "Gamma"): these models are fitted with R code, with the sparse Cholesky factorizations of the Matrix package (CHOLMOD).

bayes

Whether to fit a Bayesian version of the PGLMM using r-inla. We recommend against Bayesian fitting for non-Gaussian data unless sample sizes are large (>1000), because the phylogenetic variance tends to get trapped near zero.

reltol

A control parameter dictating the relative tolerance for convergence in the optimization; see optim. With sparse = TRUE, the default is 1e-8 (for each run of the optimizer, including each PQL iteration of binomial and poisson models). With method = "Laplace", the relative tolerance of nlminb() (default 1e-10); maxit is then its maximum number of iterations and evaluations.

maxit

A control parameter dictating the maximum number of iterations in the optimization; see optim.

tol.pql

A control parameter dictating the tolerance for convergence in the PQL estimates of the mean components of the GLMM. Ignored if family = "gaussian", bayes = TRUE, or method = "Laplace".

maxit.pql

A control parameter dictating the maximum number of iterations in the PQL estimates of the mean components of the GLMM. Ignored if family = "gaussian" or bayes = TRUE.

marginal.summ

Summary statistic to use for the estimate of coefficients when doing a Bayesian PGLMM (when bayes = TRUE). Options are: "mean", "median", or "mode", referring to different characterizations of the central tendency of the Bayesian posterior marginal distributions. Ignored if bayes = FALSE.

calc.DIC

Should the Deviance Information Criterion be calculated and returned when doing a Bayesian PGLMM? Ignored if bayes = FALSE.

prior

Which type of default prior should be used by pglmm? Only used if bayes = TRUE. There are currently four options: "inla.default", which uses the default INLA priors; "pc.prior.auto", which uses a complexity penalizing prior (as described in Simpson et al. (2017)) designed to automatically choose good parameters (only available for gaussian and binomial responses); "pc.prior", which allows the user to set custom parameters on the "pc.prior" prior, using the prior_alpha and prior_mu parameters (Run INLA::inla.doc("pc.prec") for details on these parameters); and "uninformative", which sets a very uninformative prior (nearly uniform) by using a very flat exponential distribution. The last option is generally not recommended but may in some cases give estimates closer to the maximum likelihood estimates. "pc.prior.auto" is only implemented for family = "gaussian" and family = "binomial" currently.

prior_alpha

Only used if bayes = TRUE and prior = "pc.prior", in which case it sets the alpha parameter of INLA's complexity penalizing prior for the random effects. The prior is an exponential distribution where prob(sd > mu) = alpha, where sd is the standard deviation of the random effect.

prior_mu

Only used if bayes = TRUE and prior = "pc.prior", in which case it sets the mu parameter of INLA's complexity penalizing prior for the random effects. The prior is an exponential distribution where prob(sd > mu) = alpha, where sd is the standard deviation of the random effect.

ML.init

Only relevant if bayes = TRUE. Should maximum likelihood estimates be calculated and used as initial values for the Bayesian model fit? Sometimes this can be helpful, but it may not help; thus, we set the default to FALSE. Also, it does not work with the zero-inflated families.

s2.init

Initial estimate of s2 (default 1; NULL uses the defaults of pglmm()).

B.init

Initial estimates of \(B\), a matrix containing regression coefficients in the model for the fixed effects. This matrix must have dim(B.init) = c(p + 1, 1), where p is the number of predictor (independent) variables; the first element of B corresponds to the intercept, and the remaining elements correspond in order to the predictor (independent) variables in the formula. If B.init is not provided, these are estimated using lm or glm assuming no phylogenetic signal. A better approach might be to run lmer and use the output fixed effects for B.init. When bayes = TRUE, initial values are estimated using the maximum likelihood fit unless ML.init = FALSE, in which case the default INLA initial values will be used.

calc.WAIC

Should the WAIC be calculated and returned when doing a Bayesian PGLMM? Ignored if bayes = FALSE.

bayes_options

Additional options to pass to INLA when bayes = TRUE. A named list where the names correspond to parameters in the inla function. One special option is diagonal: if an element in the list is named diagonal, INLA adds its value to the diagonal of every random-effects precision matrix, which can help with numerical stability when the model is ill-conditioned (try list(diagonal = 1e-4) if you see many warnings). To use multiple CPU cores, pass list(num.threads = 4) (or however many cores are available); this is often the single most effective way to speed up INLA. Any control.compute entries supplied here override the defaults set by posterior.sample and return.fitted.marginals.

posterior.sample

Logical (default TRUE). Only used when bayes = TRUE. When TRUE, INLA stores the full joint posterior configuration (control.compute = list(config = TRUE)), which is required for simulate to work. Set to FALSE to skip this storage and speed up fitting when posterior simulation is not needed.

return.fitted.marginals

Logical (default TRUE). Only used when bayes = TRUE. When TRUE, INLA computes and returns the marginal posterior distributions of all fitted values (control.compute = list(return.marginals.predictor = TRUE)), which is required for simulate with full = FALSE. Set to FALSE to skip this computation and speed up fitting when simulation is not needed. If both posterior.sample and return.fitted.marginals are FALSE, INLA runs at maximum speed but simulate() will not work on the fitted model.

sparse

Whether to fit the model with the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny, which is much faster for large phylogenies (see Details and pglmm()). The default, NULL, is TRUE (with bayes = TRUE, unless ML.init = TRUE; FALSE before phyr 1.5.0); use sparse = FALSE for the dense covariance matrix (then also returned in vcv.phy).

standardize_cov

Logical (default TRUE). Whether to standardize the covariance matrices of cov_ranef to have a determinant of one (a phylogeny is first converted to its covariance matrix, which is divided by its largest element). If FALSE, the matrices are used as given: a covariance matrix is used as it is, and a phylogeny gives ape::vcv(tree), on the scale of its branch lengths. The variances of the random terms (s2r, s2n) are then on the scale of these matrices, so that, e.g., the variance of 1|sp__ with a phylogenetic correlation matrix (ape::vcv(tree, corr = TRUE)) or an ultrametric tree with a height of one is directly comparable with the variance of 1|sp and with software that does not standardize the matrices. The likelihood, the fixed effects and the predictions do not depend on this choice; only the scale of the variances (and of s2.init) does. Not used when random.effects is given.

method

For binomial and poisson data, "Laplace" (default since phyr 1.5.0) or "PQL" (the default of earlier versions): see Details and pglmm(). Negative binomial and Gamma data are always fitted with "Laplace".

object

A fitted model with class pglmm_compare.

newdata

An optional data frame of species to predict for, as for predict.communityPGLMM(). The species are the row names of newdata (or its column sp), which must be tip labels of phy; with re.form = NA, they are not needed.

...

Additional arguments passed to predict.communityPGLMM().

Value

An object of class c("pglmm_compare", "communityPGLMM"): all the elements returned by pglmm() (see its Value section), and:

formula

the formula for fixed effects, as given

phy

the phylogeny, with the tips not in the data dropped

vcv.phy

a list with the (standardized) covariance matrix of the species in the order of the rows of the data, covar; NULL with sparse = TRUE

LRT

for bayes = FALSE, the test of phylogenetic signal: a list with the likelihood ratio LR, df, and the p-value Pr (see Details)

sp_var

the name of the column of species added to the data

The elements most often used are:

B, B.se, B.cov, B.zscore, B.pvalue

estimates of the regression coefficients, their approximate standard errors, covariance matrix, Z scores and p-values (B.se, B.zscore and B.pvalue are NULL if bayes = TRUE)

B.ci

credible intervals of the regression coefficients if bayes = TRUE

s2n

the phylogenetic variance s2 (and the variance of 1|obs if add.obs.re = TRUE)

s2resid

for gaussian data, the residual variance

s2n.ci, s2resid.ci

credible intervals of the variances if bayes = TRUE

logLik, AIC, BIC

the (restricted, if REML = TRUE) log-likelihood and the information criteria; with bayes = TRUE, logLik is the marginal log-likelihood, and DIC and WAIC are returned

H, mu, Y, X

residuals, predicted mean values (binomial and poisson data), response and design matrix, as in pglmm()

convcode, niter

convergence code and number of iterations of the optimizer

inla.model

the model fitted by inla, if bayes = TRUE

Details

pglmm_compare in the package phyr is similar to binaryPGLMM in the package ape, although it has much broader functionality, including accepting more than just binary data, implementing Bayesian analyses, etc.

For non-Gaussian data, the function estimates parameters for the model

$$Pr(Y = 1) = \theta $$ $$\theta = inverse.link(b0 + b1 * x1 + b2 * x2 + \dots + \epsilon)$$ $$\epsilon ~ Gaussian(0, s2 * V) $$

where \(V\) is a covariance matrix derived from a phylogeny (typically under the assumption of Brownian motion evolution). Although mathematically there is no requirement for \(V\) to be ultrametric, forcing \(V\) into ultrametric form can aide in the interpretation of the model. This is especially true for binary data, because in regression for binary dependent variables, only the off-diagonal elements (i.e., covariances) of matrix \(V\) are biologically meaningful (see Ives & Garland 2014). The function converts a phylo tree object into a covariance matrix, and further standardizes this matrix to have determinant = 1 (unless standardize_cov = FALSE). This in effect standardizes the interpretation of the scalar s2. Although mathematically not required, it is a very good idea to standardize the predictor (independent) variables to have mean 0 and variance 1. This will make the function more robust and improve the interpretation of the regression coefficients.

For Gaussian data, the function estimates parameters for the model

$$Y = b0 + b1 * x1 + b2 * x2 + \dots + \epsilon)$$ $$\epsilon ~ Gaussian(0, s2 * V + s2resid * I) $$

where \(s2resid * I\) gives the non-phylogenetic residual variance. Note that this is equivalent to a model with Pagel's lambda transformation.

pglmm_compare(Y ~ X, data = data, phy = phy) fits the same model as pglmm(Y ~ X + (1 | sp__), data = data, cov_ranef = list(sp = phy)) with a column sp of species (the row names of data), but without the non-phylogenetic random term (1 | sp) that pglmm() adds with (1 | sp__): with one row per species, that term would be confounded with the residual variance (gaussian data) or with the observation-level random term (binomial and poisson data). The phylogenetic random term is named 1|sp__ in the output of methods such as VarCorr() and ranef(). (If data already has a column sp that is not the species, the column species or .sp is used instead; its name is in sp_var.)

The returned object has class c("pglmm_compare", "communityPGLMM"), so the methods for models fitted by pglmm() can be used: fixef(), ranef() (the estimates of the phylogenetic random effect of each species, with condVar = TRUE for their standard deviations), VarCorr(), fitted(), residuals(), predict() (with newdata, the species are the row names of newdata), simulate(), logLik() and AIC() (bayes = FALSE), pglmm_profile_LRT() and pglmm_iV().

Test of phylogenetic signal. For models fitted with bayes = FALSE, the element LRT is pglmm_profile_LRT(fit, re.number = 1): a likelihood ratio test of the hypothesis that the phylogenetic variance s2 is zero, conditional on the other estimates (the log-likelihood is compared with the one obtained by setting s2 to zero, without re-estimating the other parameters). As s2 = 0 is on the boundary of the parameter space, the p-value Pr is half of the p-value of a chi-square distribution with one degree of freedom. For binomial and poisson data, the log-likelihood is the Laplace approximation of the log-likelihood (with method = "Laplace", the default) or the approximate log-likelihood of the penalized quasi-likelihood fit (with method = "PQL"). It is printed by summary().

Binary and count data. With method = "Laplace" (the default), binomial and poisson models are fitted with the Laplace approximation of the likelihood instead of penalized quasi-likelihood (PQL), which underestimates the phylogenetic variance (and with it the phylogenetic signal) for binary data; see the argument method of pglmm(). The estimates are then the same as those of glmmTMB() with a phylogenetic covariance matrix (propto()), with REML = FALSE.

Large phylogenies. With sparse = TRUE, the model is fitted with the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny (including its internal nodes) instead of the dense covariance matrix of the species; the likelihood is the same, but time and memory grow about linearly with the number of species, so data with tens of thousands of species can be fitted. See the argument sparse of pglmm() for details. The covariance matrix vcv.phy is then not formed (it is NULL); the same with method = "Laplace".

References

Ives, A. R. and Helmus, M. R. (2011) Generalized linear mixed models for phylogenetic analyses of community structure. Ecological Monographs, 81, 511–525.

Ives, A. R. and Garland, T., Jr. (2014) Phylogenetic regression for binary dependent variables. Pages 231–261 in L. Z. Garamszegi, editor. Modern Phylogenetic Comparative Methods and Their Application in Evolutionary Biology. Springer-Verlag, Berlin Heidelberg.

See also

pglmm; package ape and its function binaryPGLMM; package phylolm and its function phyloglm; package MCMCglmm

Author

Anthony R. Ives

Examples


## Illustration of `pglmm_compare` with simulated data

# Generate random phylogeny

library(ape)

n <- 100
phy <- compute.brlen(rtree(n=n), method = "Grafen", power = 1)

# Generate random data and standardize to have mean 0 and variance 1
X1 <- rTraitCont(phy, model = "BM", sigma = 1)
X1 <- (X1 - mean(X1))/var(X1)

# Simulate binary Y
sim.dat <- data.frame(Y = array(0, dim = n), X1 = X1, row.names = phy$tip.label)
sim.dat$Y <- ape::binaryPGLMM.sim(Y ~ X1, phy = phy, data=sim.dat, s2 = 1,
                             B = matrix(c(0, .25), nrow = 2, ncol = 1), 
                             nrep = 1)$Y

# Fit model
fit <- pglmm_compare(Y ~ X1, family = "binomial", phy = phy, data = sim.dat)
fit
#> Generalized linear mixed model for binomial data fit by Laplace approximation (restricted maximum likelihood)
#> 
#> Formula: Y ~ X1
#> 
#> logLik    AIC    BIC 
#> -53.88 113.75 121.57 
#> 
#> Phylogenetic random effects variance (s2):
#>    Variance Std.Dev
#> s2  0.07435  0.2727
#> 
#> Test of phylogenetic signal (H0: s2 = 0, conditional likelihood ratio test):
#>      LR      df      Pr 
#> 0.99916 1.00000 0.07874 
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>                Value Std.Error  Zscore Pvalue  
#> (Intercept)  1.19347   0.70153  1.7012 0.0889 .
#> X1          -0.23613   0.38671 -0.6106 0.5415  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 

# test of phylogenetic signal (also printed above)
fit$LRT
#> $LR
#> [1] 0.9991597
#> 
#> $df
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $Pr
#> [1] 0.07873686
#> 
# methods of pglmm() models
fixef(fit)
#>                  Value Std.Error     Zscore     Pvalue
#> (Intercept)  1.1934685 0.7015265  1.7012451 0.08889698
#> X1          -0.2361262 0.3867145 -0.6105956 0.54146737
VarCorr(fit)
#>          Variance  Std.Dev
#> 1|sp__ 0.07434785 0.272668
head(ranef(fit, condVar = TRUE)[["1|sp__"]])
#>    sp     estimate        se
#> 1 t63 -0.062401634 0.6609444
#> 2 t62 -0.051647785 0.6529569
#> 3 t48  0.007757497 0.6250426
#> 4  t8  0.020070115 0.6192487
#> 5  t3  0.019988029 0.6192830
#> 6  t6  0.018241553 0.6201783
predict(fit, newdata = sim.dat[1:3, ], type = "response")
#>         Y_hat
#> t63 0.7990353
#> t62 0.8049363
#> t48 0.8262815

# the same model fitted with the sparse precision matrix of the phylogeny,
# much faster for large phylogenies
fit_sparse <- pglmm_compare(Y ~ X1, family = "binomial", phy = phy, data = sim.dat,
                            sparse = TRUE)
cbind(dense = fit$B[, 1], sparse = fit_sparse$B[, 1])
#>                  dense     sparse
#> (Intercept)  1.1934685  1.1934685
#> X1          -0.2361262 -0.2361262

# the Laplace approximation of the likelihood (less biased than PQL for
# binary data), with maximum likelihood estimates
fit_laplace <- pglmm_compare(Y ~ X1, family = "binomial", phy = phy, data = sim.dat,
                             method = "Laplace", REML = FALSE)
fit_laplace
#> Generalized linear mixed model for binomial data fit by Laplace approximation (maximum likelihood)
#> 
#> Formula: Y ~ X1
#> 
#> logLik    AIC    BIC 
#> -53.63 113.26 121.07 
#> 
#> Phylogenetic random effects variance (s2):
#>    Variance Std.Dev
#> s2        0       0
#> 
#> Test of phylogenetic signal (H0: s2 = 0, conditional likelihood ratio test):
#>        LR        df        Pr 
#> 4.099e-11 1.000e+00 1.000e+00 
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>               Value Std.Error Zscore    Pvalue    
#> (Intercept) 1.21725   0.23945 5.0835 3.705e-07 ***
#> X1          0.14894   0.19197 0.7759    0.4378    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 

# Compare with `binaryPGLMM`
ape::binaryPGLMM(Y ~ X1, phy = phy, data = sim.dat)
#> 
#> 
#> Call:Y ~ X1
#> <environment: 0x75e30fbab8>
#> 
#> Random effect (phylogenetic signal s2):
#>      s2       Pr
#> 1 1.143 0.009459
#> 
#> Fixed effects:
#>                Value Std.Error  Zscore  Pvalue  
#> (Intercept)  1.18937   0.65263  1.8224 0.06839 .
#> X1          -0.20599   0.37001 -0.5567 0.57772  
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 

# Compare with `phyloglm`
if (requireNamespace("phylolm", quietly = TRUE)) {
  summary(phylolm::phyloglm(Y ~ X1, phy = phy, data = sim.dat))
}
#> Warning: the estimate of 'alpha' (54.5271382266451) reached the upper bound (54.5981500331442).
#>  This may simply reflect a flat likelihood at large alpha values,
#>  meaning that the phylogenetic correlation is estimated to be negligible.
#> Warning: phyloglm failed to converge.
#> 
#> Call:
#> phylolm::phyloglm(formula = Y ~ X1, data = sim.dat, phy = phy)
#>        AIC     logLik Pen.logLik 
#>     117.34     -55.67     -52.73 
#> 
#> Method: logistic_MPLE
#> Mean tip height: 1
#> Parameter estimate(s):
#> alpha: 54.52714 
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate  StdErr z.value   p.value    
#> (Intercept)  1.04492 0.25802  4.0497 5.129e-05 ***
#> X1           0.12907 0.20651  0.6250     0.532    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1
#> 
#> Note: Wald-type p-values for coefficients, conditional on alpha=54.52714
#> 

# Compare with `glm` that does not account for phylogeny
summary(glm(Y ~ X1, data = sim.dat, family = "binomial"))
#> 
#> Call:
#> glm(formula = Y ~ X1, family = "binomial", data = sim.dat)
#> 
#> Coefficients:
#>             Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
#> (Intercept)   1.2173     0.2395   5.084 3.71e-07 ***
#> X1            0.1489     0.1920   0.776    0.438    
#> ---
#> Signif. codes:  0 ‘***’ 0.001 ‘**’ 0.01 ‘*’ 0.05 ‘.’ 0.1 ‘ ’ 1

#> Residual deviance: 107.26  on 98  degrees of freedom
#> AIC: 111.26
#> 
#> Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4
#> 

# Compare with logistf() that does not account
# for phylogeny but is less biased than glm()
if (requireNamespace("logistf", quietly = TRUE)) {
  logistf::logistf(Y ~ X1, data = sim.dat)
}
#> logistf::logistf(formula = Y ~ X1, data = sim.dat)
#> Model fitted by Penalized ML
#> Confidence intervals and p-values by Profile Likelihood 
#>

#>   1.1881861   0.1477537

#> Likelihood ratio test=0.6131352 on 1 df, p=0.4336098, n=100
#> 

## Fit model with bayes = TRUE
# pglmm_compare(Y ~ X1, family = "binomial", phy = phy, data = sim.dat, 
#               bayes = TRUE, calc.DIC = TRUE)

# Compare with `MCMCglmm`

V <- vcv(phy)
V <- V/max(V)
detV <- exp(determinant(V)$modulus[1])
V <- V/detV^(1/n)

invV <- Matrix::Matrix(solve(V),sparse = TRUE)
sim.dat$species <- phy$tip.label
rownames(invV) <- sim.dat$species

nitt <- 43000
thin <- 10
burnin <- 3000

prior <- list(R=list(V=1, fix=1), G=list(G1=list(V=1, nu=1000, alpha.mu=0, alpha.V=1)))
# commented out to save time
# summary(MCMCglmm::MCMCglmm(Y ~ X1, random = ~species, ginvers = list(species = invV),
#     data = sim.dat, slice = TRUE, nitt = nitt, thin = thin, burnin = burnin,
#    family = "categorical", prior = prior, verbose = FALSE))
